content: Following a period of mechanical ventilation, newborn infants may develop upper airway obstruction after extubation. This is particularly common in cases where intubation was prolonged, traumatic, or performed multiple times. Such obstruction increases upper airway resistance, which can lead to respiratory insufficiency and failure of extubation. Epinephrine, due to its vasoconstrictive properties, has been shown to be effective in treating croup in infants. Consequently, some neonatal units routinely administer nebulized epinephrine immediately after extubation. Additionally, neonatal and respiratory textbooks and reviews recommend its use for neonates experiencing post-extubation tracheal obstruction and stridor. The primary aim of this review was to determine whether administering nebulized epinephrine immediately after extubation in neonates weaned from intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) reduces the need for additional respiratory support. To address this, searches were conducted in multiple databases, including MEDLINE (1966 to September 2000), CINAHL (1982 to September 2000), Current Contents (1994 to September 2000), and the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register (Issue 3, 2000). These searches were updated to September 2001 and again in December 2009. Earlier searches up to March 1999 also included the Oxford Database of Perinatal Trials, expert informants, hand-searching of journals, cross-references from previous reviews, abstracts, and conference proceedings. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing nebulized epinephrine with placebo in newborn infants who had been weaned from IPPV and extubated. The outcomes of interest included the need for additional respiratory support, increased oxygen requirements, respiratory distress, stridor, and the occurrence of side effects. No studies meeting these criteria were identified. As a result, there is no evidence available to evaluate the effect of nebulized epinephrine on clinically significant outcomes in extubated newborn infants. The authors concluded that there is currently no evidence to either support or refute the use of inhaled nebulized racemic epinephrine in newborn infants. They emphasized the need for randomized controlled trials to compare nebulized epinephrine with placebo in neonates post-extubation. Such studies should evaluate its use both as a routine treatment after extubation and as a specific intervention for post-extubation upper airway obstruction. The study populations should include infants at the highest risk for upper airway obstruction due to mucosal swelling, particularly those with birth weights under 1000 grams, as their small glottic and subglottic diameters make them more vulnerable.
